definition: Collaborative search engines (CSE) are web search engines and enterprise searches within company intranets that let users combine their efforts in information retrieval (IR) activities, share information resources collaboratively using knowledge tags, and allow experts to guide less experienced people through their searches.
details: Collaboration partners do so by providing query terms, collective tagging, adding comments or opinions, rating search results, and links clicked of former (successful) IR activities to users having the same or a related information need.

explainer.lead: A collaborative search engine turns searching from a solitary activity into shared work. People can contribute queries, tags, comments, ratings, and useful trails of clicked links so that others with a related information need can search with more guidance.

tiers.eli5: Imagine looking for a lost book with friends instead of searching alone. Each person can suggest words to try, leave notes about where they looked, and mark which clues helped. A collaborative search engine does something similar for web or company searches, and an experienced searcher can show others a useful path.
tiers.practitioner: This approach applies to web search and enterprise search on company intranets, where the system records and shares search contributions around common or related information needs. Useful signals include suggested query terms, collective tags, comments, result ratings, and links selected during earlier successful searches. A key design pitfall is presenting another person's activity as relevant when the underlying information need is actually different.
tiers.paperLevel: A collaborative search engine can be described as CSE = IR + shared search contributions + optional expert guidance, where the contributions include query terms, collective tags, comments or opinions, result ratings, and clicked links from previous successful IR activities. Reuse is conditioned on users having the same or a related information need. Its scope includes both web search engines and enterprise search within company intranets.

explainer.example: Several employees need instructions for configuring an internal service. One suggests better query terms, another tags a useful intranet page and rates it highly, and a third leaves a comment explaining why it helped; an expert then points a newer colleague toward the query and links that succeeded earlier.

usedIn.name: Web search
usedIn.detail: Searchers can pool queries and judgments about results rather than working entirely independently.

usedIn.name: Company intranets
usedIn.detail: Employees can share useful resources and search trails for related workplace information needs.

usedIn.name: Expert-guided research
usedIn.detail: Experienced searchers can guide less experienced people through their information-retrieval activities.

explainer.intuition: A successful search contains knowledge beyond its final answer: the words tried, resources found, judgments made, and path followed. A collaborative search engine preserves and shares that knowledge so other people do not have to rediscover it alone.
howItWorks: Users search individually or together for information.
They contribute query terms, knowledge tags, comments, or result ratings.
The system also makes clicked links from earlier successful searches available for reuse.
People with the same or a related information need draw on these shared contributions.
Experts can guide less experienced users through the search process.
explainer.whyItMatters: It lets people build on earlier search effort instead of repeatedly starting from scratch. It also provides a way to share resources collectively and transfer practical search guidance from experts to less experienced users.
misconceptions: It is not merely several people searching at the same time; their contributions must be shared.
It is not limited to tagging, since queries, comments, ratings, and clicked links can also contribute.
Shared activity is useful for the same or a related information need, not automatically for every search.
